case_data.title: Citizen's Assembly on AI - French Speaking Switzerland
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
The 2025 Citizen's Assembly on AI in French Speaking Switzerland was organized in November 2025 by the EPFL AI Center in collaboration with the Research Hub on Democratic Innovations at the University of Geneva and Demoscan. 

The project included a survey of 734 residents of French-speaking Switzerland and a deliberation process with 40 randomly selected citizens from French speaking Switzerland, reflecting the demographics of the population, who met over a total of four days on two weekends, hearing from experts and deliberating to explore their views on AI.  

It resulted in 20 proposals that outline the foundations of responsible AI governance, including proposals on privacy protection, transparency, and meaningful human control.
case_data.what-limitations-to-the-project-should-b:
The project report notes a number of methodological limitations that impacted the project. A low 10% response rate on the initial survey due to tight deadlines and the technical nature of artificial intelligence. Additionally, a notable "volunteer effect" emerged among those willing to commit to the four-day, in-person format, creating an initial pool that skewed toward tertiary-educated individuals, residents of the canton of Vaud, and left-of-center political alignments. 

Organizers used a weighted lottery to correct these imbalances, the small size of the final assembly (40 participants) meant that random dropouts and subsequent replacements still caused minor geographic skews, such as an overrepresentation of the canton of Jura and an underrepresentation of Neuchâtel.  

Practical constraints of the format restricted participation to those available on weekends, and the entire project was structurally limited to the French-speaking regions of Switzerland, meaning it did not capture the perspectives of the rest of the country.
case_data.headline-findings:
The Citizens Assembly component resulted in five issues, and two objectives, and a set of supporting recommendations for society and policy makers. 

The issues and objectives are detailed bellow, and the more detailed recommendations can found in the full report. 

ISSUE 1: Determine the degree of state involvement and responsibility in AI, in its development and implementation in Switzerland.  

Objective 1: Adopt a national AI strategy.  

Objective 2: Promote the development of AI in accordance with human rights, enriched by Swiss values, in order to shape the future of AI.  

ISSUE 2: Democratize access to AI and promote equality, encourage healthy, responsible and ethical use, notably to limit dependency and foster social interactions, including in the real world.  

Objective 1: Raise public awareness of AI, train people in its responsible use, and facilitate access for everyone.  

Objective 2: Promote social, cultural, sporting and artistic gatherings so as not to fall into an "all-AI" world.  

ISSUE 3: Prepare the world of work for the AI transition with regard to social and financial protection and to technological changes in jobs.  

Objective 1: Anticipate the socio-professional impacts linked to the advent of AI.  

Objective 2: Guarantee dignity, and human and financial support, for people who may lose their job or experience a change in their role due to AI.  

ISSUE 4: Guarantee the origin and traceability of outputs and distinguish what comes from humans from what comes from AI.  

Objective 1: Label human creation.  

Objective 2: Adapt and strengthen copyright protection.  

ISSUE 5: Define responsible and ethical practices for AI users (legal entities and natural persons) that guarantee data protection and the reliability of tools shared online.  

Objective 1: Define criteria for good practices for users and providers and create instruments (national labeling body, legislation, etc.) to implement and assess these good practices.  

Objective 2: Fight cybercrime.
case_data.inclusion-efforts:
The project ensured accessibility and inclusion by using a weighted random lottery (sortition) to select the final 40 participants from a volunteer pool, intentionally correcting demographic skews to mirror the general population's mix of age, sex, geographic cantons, political alignments, and education levels. 

To foster an inclusive deliberative environment for laypeople tackling a complex technical topic, expert presentations were designed to be factual and accessible. Furthermore, facilitators utilised specific group-dynamic exercises on the second day—such as "the power walk"—to raise awareness about moral equality and address potential asymmetries in speaking time, while participants collectively established ground rules to guarantee balanced, respectful dialogue.
case_data.project-title: Citizen's Assembly on AI - French Speaking Switzerland
case_data.why-is-this-project-important-to-include: The project reflects an academic-led process within a specific language community in Switzerland. The team frame the work as " a compass for policymakers and civil society alike", with the goal of influencing public debate on AI governance.
project-goals: Quantitative: Generate statistical evidence on public attitudes to AI
Qualitative: Capture qualitative evidence on public attitudes to AI

do-any-of-the-following-apply: There was a learning phase for participants
data.additional-notes: The process was designed and facilitated by Demoscan to ensure democratic innovation and strict neutrality. The assembly followed a structured 4-day progression: Day 1 was dedicated to expert input and a learning phase; Day 2 involved problem framing and identifying major issues; Day 3 focused on defining operational objectives; and Day 4 concluded with drafting and voting on the final 20 proposals. An exit survey showed a very high participant satisfaction rate and a strong endorsement of the process's neutrality.
data.recruitment-description: Of the 734 people responding to the online survey, one quarter (24%) indicated that they wished to participate in the Assembly. From these volunteers, 40 citizens were selected, with the aim, as far as possible, of ensuring balanced representation across cantons, sexes, education levels, ages and political orientations.

data.name: Citizen's Assembly on AI - French Speaking Switzerland-Online survey
data.additional-notes: The survey yielded a response rate of approximately 10%. It served to establish an initial snapshot of public opinion on AI in French-speaking Switzerland before the deliberative phase began.
data.recruitment-description: The Federal Statistical Office provided 7,000 randomly selected addresses from all French-speaking cantons/regions, ensuring a balance across sex and age groups (16+). These individuals received an invitation letter by post to complete the survey online. 734 participants responded.
